items.stem:
Eiffel Tower : The Eiffel Tower is a landmark and an early example of wrought-iron construction on a gigantic scale. The lower section consists of four immense arched legs set on masonry piers. The legs curve inward until they unite in a single tapered tower. Platforms, each with an observation deck, are at three levels; on the first is also a restaurant.
The tower, constructed of about 7000 tons of iron, has stairs and elevators. A meteorological station, a radio communications station, and a television transmission antenna, as well as a suite of rooms that were used by Eiffel are located near the top of the tower.
(i) For a person standing 324 m from the center of the base of the Eiffel Tower, the angle of elevation to the top of the tower is 45°. How tall is the Eiffel Tower?
(ii) A car is moving at uniform speed towards the Eiffel tower. It takes 15 minutes for the angle of depression from the top of tower to the car to change from 30° to 60°. After how much time after this, the car will reach the base of the tower?
items.answer:
(i) Let h be the height of the tower. From the person's position, tan 45° = h/324, so 1 = h/324 and h = 324 m.
(ii) Let d be the car's distance from the foot of the tower when the depression is 30°. Then tan 30° = 324/d, so d = 324√3 m. When the depression has grown to 60°, the remaining distance d₂ satisfies tan 60° = 324/d₂, so d₂ = 324/√3 = 108√3 m. The car therefore covered d₁ = 324√3 − 108√3 = 216√3 m in 15 minutes, and 216√3 = 2 × 108√3, so the remaining 108√3 m is exactly half that journey. At the same uniform speed it takes 15 ÷ 2 = 7.5 minutes. The Eiffel Tower is 324 m tall and the car reaches its base 7.5 minutes after the second sighting.
items.ocr: A photograph of the Eiffel Tower is printed with the question; it is decorative and carries no measurement, so it is not attached.

items.stem:
From the observation deck of a seaside building 200 m high, Jignesh sees two fishing boats in the distance. The angle of depression to the nearer boat is 60° while for the boat farther away the angle is 45°.
(i) How far out to sea is the nearer boat?
(ii) How far apart are the two boats?
items.answer:
Let d₁ be the distance of the nearer boat from the foot of the building and d₂ the further gap out to the second boat. The deck is 200 m above sea level.
(i) For the nearer boat, tan 60° = 200/d₁, so d₁ = 200/√3 = 200√3/3 ≈ 115.47 m. The nearer boat is about 115.47 m out to sea.
(ii) For the farther boat, tan 45° = 200/(d₁ + d₂), so d₁ + d₂ = 200 m. Hence d₂ = 200 − 115.47 = 84.53 m. The two boats are about 84.53 m apart.
items.ocr: Key contradicted. The stem and the solution's own diagram both give the deck height as 200 m, but the printed algebra substitutes 150 (tan 60° = 150/d₁) and so reports 86.6 m and 63.4 m. Recomputed from the printed 200 m: 115.47 m and 84.53 m. A drawing of the lighthouse and the two boats is printed between question and solution; it repeats only the 60° and 45° already in the stem, so it is not attached.

items.stem: While doing some night fishing, Sarthak round a peninsula and a tall light house comes into view. Taking a sighting, Sarthak find the angle of elevation to the top of the lighthouse is 30°. If the lighthouse is known to be 25 m tall, how far from the lighthouse is Sarthak ?
items.answer: Let d be the horizontal distance between Sarthak and the foot of the lighthouse. The lighthouse is 25 m tall and is seen at an elevation of 30°, so tan 30° = 25/d, that is 1/√3 = 25/d. Hence d = 25√3 = 25 × 1.732 = 43.3 m. Sarthak is about 43.3 metre away from the lighthouse.
items.ocr: A night scene of the lighthouse and boat is printed with the question; it carries no measurement and is not attached.

items.stem:
On a warm and lazy Saturday, Rishi is watching a county maintenance crew mow the park across the street. He notices the mower takes 16 sec to pass through 60° of rotation from one end of the park to the other. If the corner of the park is 40 meter directly across the street from his house,
(i) How wide is the park?
(ii) How fast (in kmph) does the mower travel as it cuts the grass?
items.answer:
(i) Rishi's line to the near corner of the park is 40 m long and is perpendicular to the width of the park, and the mower sweeps 60° from that line to the far corner. So tan 60° = w/40, giving w = 40√3 = 40 × 1.732 = 69.28 m. The park is about 69.28 metre wide.
(ii) The mower covers that width in 16 seconds, so its speed is s = 69.28/16 = 4.33 m/sec. Converting, 4.33 × 3.6 = 15.6 km/h. The mower travels at about 15.6 kmph.
items.ocr: An illustration of the street and park is printed inside the question; it only repeats the 60° given in the text, so it is not attached.

items.stem:
Speed Limit Enforcement : Rajendra works in traffic police and manage traffic on highway. His van is having radar detection equipment. He takes up a hidden position 50 meter from the highway. Using a sighting device he finds the angle between his position and a road sign in the distance is 60°. He then uses a stop watch to determine how long it takes a vehicle to pass her location and reach the road sign. In quick succession—an 18-wheeler, a truck, and a car pass her position, with the time each takes to travel this distance noted. Find the speed of each vehicle in miles per hour if
(i) the 18-wheeler takes 8 sec,
(ii) the truck takes 6 sec,
(iii) the car takes 4 sec.
items.answer:
Let d be the length of road between the point opposite the van and the road sign. The van sits 50 m off the highway and sights the sign at 60° from that perpendicular, so tan 60° = d/50 and d = 50√3 = 50 × 1.732 = 86.6 m.
(i) 18-wheeler: s₁ = 86.6/8 = 10.825 m/sec = 10.825 × 3.6 = 38.97 km/h.
(ii) Truck: s₂ = 86.6/6 = 14.43 m/sec = 14.43 × 3.6 = 51.96 km/h.
(iii) Car: s₃ = 86.6/4 = 21.65 m/sec = 21.65 × 3.6 = 77.94 km/h.
items.ocr: The stem asks for speeds 'in miles per hour' but every quantity in the question and the whole printed solution are metric; the answers are given in km/h as the solution does. A highway illustration repeating the printed 50 m and 60° is not attached.

items.stem: Rainbow: While visiting the Mount Abu in Rajasthan, Taniya and Lavanya see a spectacularly vivid rainbow arching over the lake. Taniya speculates the rainbow is 250 m away, while Lavanya estimates the angle of elevation to the highest point of the rainbow is about 60°. What was the approximate height of the rainbow?
items.answer: Let h be the height of the highest point of the rainbow above the girls' level. The horizontal distance to that point is 250 m and it is seen at an elevation of 60°, so tan 60° = h/250, that is √3 = h/250. Hence h = 250√3 = 250 × 1.732 ≈ 433 m. The rainbow rises to about 433 metre.
items.ocr: The printed working writes '250 × 1.173' — a misprint for 1.732 — and rounds to 432.5 m; 250√3 is 433.01, so 433 m is given here. A photograph of a rainbow is printed with the question and is not attached.

items.stem:
CN Tower : The tallest free-standing tower in the world is the CN Tower in Toronto, Canada. The tower includes a rotating restaurant high above the ground. From a distance of 208 meter the angle of elevation to the pinnacle of the tower is 60°. The angle of elevation to the restaurant from the same vantage point is 45°.
(i) How tall is the CN Tower?
(ii) How far below the pinnacle of the tower is the restaurant located?
items.answer:
Let h₁ be the height of the pinnacle and h₂ the height of the restaurant, both measured from the vantage point's level, which is 208 m from the foot of the tower.
(i) tan 60° = h₁/208, so h₁ = 208√3 = 208 × 1.73 ≈ 360 m. The CN Tower is about 360 metre tall.
(ii) tan 45° = h₂/208, so h₂ = 208 m. The restaurant therefore lies 360 − 208 = 152 m below the pinnacle.
items.ocr: A photograph of the CN Tower is printed with the question; it carries no measurement and is not attached.

items.stem: Height of Cloud Cover : To measure the height of the cloud cover at an airport, a worker shines a spotlight upward at an angle 45° from the horizontal. An observer 600 m away measures the angle of elevation to the spot of light to be 30°. Find the height of the cloud cover.
items.answer: Let h be the height of the lit spot on the cloud above the ground, let d₁ be the observer's horizontal distance from the point below the spot and d₂ the spotlight's. From the observer, tan 30° = h/d₁, so d₁ = √3 h. From the spotlight, tan 45° = h/d₂, so d₂ = h. The spotlight and the observer are 600 m apart, so d₁ + d₂ = 600, giving √3 h + h = 600 and (√3 + 1)h = 600. Hence h = 600/(√3 + 1) = 600(√3 − 1)/2 = 300(1.732 − 1) = 300 × 0.732 = 219.6 m. The cloud cover is about 219.6 metre high.
items.ocr: A grey photograph of the spotlight scene is printed with the question; its labels are illegible and it carries no data beyond the stem, so it is not attached.

items.stem: Use the diagram given to derive a formula for the height h of the taller building in terms of the height x of the shorter building and the ratios for tan θ and tan φ.
items.answer:
In the diagram, d is the distance between the two buildings, φ is the angle of elevation of the top of the taller building measured from the foot of the shorter one, and θ is its angle of elevation measured from the top of the shorter building, whose height is x.
From the foot of the shorter building, tan φ = h/d, so d = h/tan φ.
From the top of the shorter building the taller one rises only h − x above eye level, so tan θ = (h − x)/d. Substituting d gives tan θ = (h − x) tan φ / h, hence h tan θ = h tan φ − x tan φ.
Collecting the h terms, h tan φ − h tan θ = x tan φ, so h(tan φ − tan θ) = x tan φ and therefore
h = x tan φ / (tan φ − tan θ).
items.ocr: The question is unanswerable without the printed diagram, which is where θ, φ, d, x and h are defined; it is attached.

items.stem: Distance Measuring Equipment : DME is standard avionic equipment on a commercial airplane. This equipment measures the distance from a plane to a radar station. If the distance from a plane to a radar station is 200 km and the angle of depression is 30°, find the ground distance from a point directly below the plane to the radar station.
items.answer: Let d be the ground distance from the point directly below the plane to the radar station. The slant line from the plane to the station is 200 km long and makes 30° with the horizontal, so the horizontal leg is the adjacent side: cos 30° = d/200, that is √3/2 = d/200. Hence d = 100√3 = 100 × 1.732 = 173.2 km. The ground distance is about 173.2 kilometre.
items.ocr: The closing line of the printed solution says '173.2 meter' although every datum is in kilometres; km is used here. The illustration beside the question labels the depression 60°, contradicting the 30° stated in the text; the text's 30° is used and the illustration is not attached.

items.stem:
Height of a Climber : Himalayan Trekking Club has just hiked to the south rim of a large canyon, when they spot a climber attempting to scale the taller northern face. Knowing the distance between the sheer walls of the northern and southern faces of the canyon is approximately 150 meter, they attempt to compute the distance remaining for the climbers to reach the top of the northern rim. Using a homemade transit, they sight an angle of depression of 60° to the bottom of the north face, and angles of elevation of 30° and 45° to the climbers and top of the northern rim respectively.
(i) How high is the southern rim of the canyon?
(ii) How high is the northern rim?
(iii) How much farther until the climber reaches the top?
items.answer:
The trekkers stand on the south rim, 150 m horizontally from the north face. Let h₁ be the height of the south rim above the canyon floor, h₂ the height of the north rim above the trekkers' eye level, and h₃ the height of the climber above that same level.
(i) Looking down at the bottom of the north face, tan 60° = h₁/150, so h₁ = 150√3 = 150 × 1.732 = 259.8 m. The southern rim is about 259.8 metre high.
(ii) Looking up at the top of the north face, tan 45° = h₂/150, so h₂ = 150 m. The northern rim therefore stands h₁ + h₂ = 259.8 + 150 = 409.8 m above the canyon floor.
(iii) Looking up at the climber, tan 30° = h₃/150, so h₃ = 150/√3 = 50√3 = 50 × 1.732 = 86.6 m. The climber still has h₂ − h₃ = 150 − 86.6 = 63.4 m to go.
items.ocr: A drawing of the canyon is printed inside the question; it only repeats the 30°, 45° and 60° already stated, so it is not attached.

items.stem:
An observer notes that the angle of elevation from point A to the top of a space shuttle is 45°. From a point 20 meters further from the space shuttle, the angle of elevation is 30°.
(i) Find the height of the space shuttle.
(ii) Find the distance of point A from space shuttle.
items.answer:
Let h be the height of the space shuttle and d the ground distance of A from its base; the second point B is 20 m beyond A on the same line.
From A, tan 45° = h/d, so 1 = h/d and h = d.
From B, tan 30° = h/(d + 20), so 1/√3 = h/(h + 20) after putting d = h. Cross-multiplying, h + 20 = √3 h, so 20 = h(√3 − 1) and h = 20/(√3 − 1) = 20(√3 + 1)/2 = 10(1.732 + 1) = 10 × 2.732 = 27.32 m.
(i) The space shuttle is 27.32 m high.
(ii) Since d = h, point A is also 27.32 m from the space shuttle.
items.ocr: An illustration of the shuttle repeating the printed 45° and 30° is not attached.

items.stem: Height of a Building : A surveyor determines that the angle of elevation from a transit to the top of a building is 30°. The transit is positioned 2 meter above ground level and 30 meter from the building. Find the height of the building.
items.answer: Let h be the height of the building measured from the level of the transit. The transit is 30 m from the building and sights the top at 30°, so tan 30° = h/30, that is 1/√3 = h/30. Hence h = 30/√3 = 10√3 = 10 × 1.732 = 17.32 m. The transit itself stands 2 m above the ground, so the building's height from the ground is 17.32 + 2 = 19.32 m.
items.ocr: A drawing of the surveyor and building repeating the printed 30° is not attached.

items.stem:
Width of a Lake : The angle of depression to one side of a lake, measured from a balloon 300 meter above the lake as shown in the accompanying figure, is 45°. The angle of depression to the opposite side of the lake is 30°.
(i) Find the width of the lake.
(ii) Find the ground distance of balloon from sides of lake.
items.answer:
Let d₁ and d₂ be the horizontal distances from the point directly below the balloon to the nearer and the farther side of the lake; the balloon floats 300 m above the water.
For the nearer side, tan 45° = 300/d₁, so 1 = 300/d₁ and d₁ = 300 m.
For the farther side, tan 30° = 300/d₂, so 1/√3 = 300/d₂ and d₂ = 300√3 = 300 × 1.732 = 519.6 m.
(i) The width of the lake is w = d₁ + d₂ = 300 + 519.6 = 819.6 m.
(ii) The ground distances of the balloon from the two sides are 300 metre and 519.6 metre.
items.ocr: The stem says 'as shown in the accompanying figure', but the printed picture only repeats the 300 m, 45° and 30° already given in words, so it is not attached.

items.stem:
Height of a Pyramid : The angle of elevation to the top of the Egyptian pyramid of Cheops is 30° measured from a point 50 meter from the base of the pyramid. The angle of elevation from the base of a face of the pyramid is 60°.
(i) Find the height of the Cheops pyramid.
(ii) Find the side of base of pyramid.
items.answer:
Let h be the height of the pyramid above the centre of its square base and let 2a be the side of that base, so that a is the horizontal distance from the centre to the middle of a face.
From the foot of the face, tan 60° = h/a, so a = h/√3.
From the point 50 m further out, tan 30° = h/(a + 50), so 1/√3 = h/(a + 50) and a + 50 = √3 h.
Substituting a = h/√3 gives h/√3 + 50 = √3 h. Multiplying by √3, h + 50√3 = 3h, so 2h = 50√3 and h = 25√3 = 25 × 1.732 = 43.3 m.
(i) The Cheops pyramid is about 43.3 metre high.
(ii) a = h/√3 = 25√3/√3 = 25 m, so the side of the base is 2a = 2 × 25 = 50 m.
items.ocr: The printed working labels the line 'h/√3 = 25 m' as 2a when it is in fact a; the book's own stated answer, side = 50 m, follows from a = 25 m, so the labelling is the slip and the answer stands. The pyramid illustration repeats the printed 30° and 60° and is not attached.

items.stem: Washington Monument : The Washington Monument is a large, tall, white obelisk near the west part of the National Mall in Washington, D.C. It was built to remember George Washington, who was the first President of the United States. It is the tallest stone structure in the world. From a point A on a line from the base of the Washington Monument, the angle of elevation to the top of the monument is 45°. From a point 125 m away from A and on the same line, the angle to the top is 30°. Find the height of the Washington Monument.
items.answer:
Let h be the height of the monument and d the ground distance of A from its base; the second point B lies 125 m further along the same line.
From A, tan 45° = h/d, so d = h.
From B, tan 30° = h/(d + 125), so 1/√3 = h/(d + 125) and d + 125 = √3 h. Putting d = h gives h + 125 = √3 h, so 125 = h(√3 − 1) and h = 125/(√3 − 1) = 125(√3 + 1)/2 = 125 × 2.732/2 = 170.75 m. The Washington Monument is about 170.75 metre high.
items.ocr: A photograph of the monument is printed with the question; it carries no measurement and is not attached.

items.stem: Fire towers : Two fire towers are 4 kilometres apart, where tower is due west of tower. A fire is spotted from the towers, and the angle of fire sight from tower is shown below. Find the distance of the fire from the line segment.
items.answer:
Let d be the perpendicular distance of the fire from the line joining the two towers, and let the foot of that perpendicular divide the 4 km into d₁ on the west side and d₂ on the east side. From the figure the fire is sighted at 30° from the western tower and 45° from the eastern tower.
From the western tower, tan 30° = d/d₁, so d₁ = √3 d.
From the eastern tower, tan 45° = d/d₂, so d₂ = d.
Since d₁ + d₂ = 4 km, √3 d + d = 4, that is (√3 + 1)d = 4. Hence d = 4/(√3 + 1) = 4(√3 − 1)/2 = 2(√3 − 1) = 2 × 0.732 = 1.46 km. The fire is about 1.46 kilometre from the line joining the towers.
items.ocr: Key contradicted. Both the question's illustration and the solution's own redrawn diagram mark the eastern angle 45°, but the printed algebra substitutes tan 60° (d₂ = d/√3) and so reports d = √3 = 1.732 km. Worked from the 45° that is actually printed, d = 2(√3 − 1) ≈ 1.46 km. The stem is transcribed as printed: the book omits the tower labels in 'tower is due west of tower' and 'the angle of fire sight from tower'. The figure carries the only statement of the two angles, so it is attached.

items.stem: Flag Pole : Figure given below is a diagram that shows how Varsha estimates the height of a flagpole. She can't measure the distance between herself and the flagpole directly because there is a fence in the way. So she stands at point A facing the pole and finds the angle of elevation from point A to the top of the pole to be 30°. Then she turns 90° and walks 15 metre to point B, where she measures the angle between her path and a line from B to the base of the pole. She finds that angle is 60°. Find the height of the pole.
items.answer:
Let C be the foot of the pole, D its top, h the height CD, and d the ground distance CA.
Varsha turns through 90° at A, so triangle ABC has its right angle at A, with AB = 15 m and the angle at B equal to 60°. Here AC is opposite that angle, so tan 60° = d/15, giving √3 = d/15 and d = 15√3 m.
Now in right triangle ACD, the pole is seen from A at 30°, so tan 30° = h/d, that is 1/√3 = h/(15√3). Hence h = 15√3/√3 = 15 m. The flagpole is 15 metre high.
items.ocr: The stem itself says 'Figure given below', and the labels A, B, C, D and the right angle at C come only from the diagram, so it is attached. The question begins on page 43 and its solution runs onto page 44.
